I shall make your offering splendid.”
The orphan mounted and set out,
Traveling farther on.
At the lower spur where the mountain ended,
At the jutting headland,
On the edge of broad Ak-Chii,
Upon the main road,
“My noble mother Kanykei—
These were the words she spoke—
My khan-father's enclosure,
She said, was at that very place.”
A lofty mausoleum came into view.
When he saw that mausoleum,
Khan Manas's orphan
Was stricken with grief,
Tears pouring from his eyes,
As though his wolf-man khan-father were watching him.
His eyes darted wildly,
His limbs weakened and hung slack.
When he saw the white mausoleum,
It seemed to him like his father.
To the city of Khan Temir
That poor child had wandered;
To the city of Karakan
He had fled and grown up.
Kanykei had been left in mourning;
Semetey had fled there,
Plundering the costly cloth and prospering.
Semetey had entered Bukhara and grown up;
Until he reached twelve,
The child had never seen the mausoleum.
His heart burned like fire.
The reason for this burning was:
“Someone may become an enemy,” she thought.
“If they call him ‘Manas's son,’
My dark eyes will be stricken blind.
The orphan left by my khan
Someone will kill,” she thought.
The twig had been cut,
The rite performed.
He had been fed the flesh of wild game,
Made to be called Ysmayyl's son.
He had not worn a proper coat.
Until he reached twelve,
That Khan Manas, gone to the other world,
Was his father, he had not known.
After the child saw the mausoleum,
His father's deeds
The orphan wished to learn truly.
With his thoughts upon them, he traveled on,
Heading toward the great mausoleum.
Seeing it, he wailed;
The child, the bereft orphan, roared,
Crying “Father!” in ringing grief.
His golden-cheeked battle-axe
He braced against his bare flank,
Circled, wept and spoke:
“Father, may you be in paradise!” he cried.
“Pledged to twelve spiritual guides,
My devastating father, have you died?
Now that I have reached twelve,
Father, have I come to you swaying with tears?
You drove white deer and made them cattle,
Threw the lands you fought into turmoil.
My lion father, have you died?
Grown up wandering far away,
Have I come, a shameless orphan?
Where two waters pour together,
Like their mighty river, my khan-father;
Where two mountains clash,
Like their great crag, my khan-father!
To your mausoleum, your palace enclosure,
Your only son has come roaring.
Father whose death grieves me, wake!
To the city of Khan Bukhara
I fled and grew up.
Is there anyone as wretched as I?
God, set my affairs right!
My departed father, support me!
Like the yellow star near dawn,
I never became a guiding sign for my father.
Learning wisdom from my bloodthirsty father,
I, the orphan, never became his companion.
Khan-father, could you not have died when I reached seven?
I never saw my khan-father's face!
Shaking the heads of grass,
Is there anything as forlorn as the wind?
Never having seen my father's face,
Is there anyone in the world as forlorn as I?
My panther father, remain undying;
Let your only son remain no orphan.
While my father Manas was alive,
I never turned the white steed's head.
Wretched soul, I never leveled a spear at the unbeliever.
Could you not have died after that, Father?
I never saw your many deeds.
While my father Manas was alive,
I never wore an armored cap,
Never leaned back and struck the enemy.
My father's battleground was great Beijing;
I never smashed them and drove them before me.
If only I could see my lion father,
And you might die after that!
To the city of Khan Temir
I wandered and lived out my days.
Is there anyone as wretched as I?
Without showing me his face,
Was my khan-father one to die like this?
A noble prince's only son—
Is there one who must wander in exile?
My valiant father, princely son,
Is there a grave for me to enter?
A prince's only son—
Is there cause for him to flee about?
My beloved khan-father,
So we may lie together,
Is there a grave beneath your arm?”
Roaring out his sorrow,
The orphan servant left by Manas
Called, “Father!”
Ysmayyl's painted spear
Against his father's mausoleum's
Threshold he struck.
Leaning on the painted spear,
He stood calling, “Father!”
Hey, as the child stood thus,
The birch wept, the willow wept,
All who watched were weeping.
Many a heart was broken;
The mausoleum's interior rumbled,
Many signs appeared.
Within the mausoleum it roared;
Within the mausoleum, hey, blessed one,
It murmured, hey, and spoke.
These were the words my mother Kanykei had spoken:
“When God truly grants his favor,
When he lays hardship upon you,
If what I say is not false,
When your father truly lends his aid,
Inside the mausoleum, hey, it will murmur;
Its signs, hey, will rumble.
If that sign is there, hey,
Go to the six villains, hey, she said.
The possessions left by your father,
Take them back openly, she said.
My foal, if there is no such sign,
Go no farther; return.
‘I saw no sign,’
Come and tell your valiant mother!”
That deed of my mother's was true.
My panther father, the bloodthirsty lion,
Saying, “My only living likeness has come, hey,”
Was lending his support.
My khan-father has left this world.
I may devote myself to Allah,
Offer myself to God.
I am grateful, hey, to my father,
And give thanks, hey, to my mother.
Your sword stands in its sheath.
What my precious mother had done,
The splendor she provided for my father,
Was indeed real and true.
Then, in the mud of broad Talas,
When the Kyrgyz lay at their ease,
My father coughing upon his pillow, ah,
Lying gravely ill, ah,
His heart sorely troubled,
All his brothers hostile,
Then that poor soul was distraught, hey.
“My panther lord will die, hey,” she thought,
“This bereft soul will know grief,” she thought.
“Allah will take my lord,” she thought.
“In this Talas, hey, there is no monument.
My beloved princely son,
Will settle beside the river, hey,” she thought.
“Not a single mark will remain.
My sultan will be like an extinguished fire, hey,” she thought.
“God will take me, ah,” she thought.
“My wolf-man will be left without a memorial,” she thought.
While my father lay ill,
My wretched mother had searched the cities,
My mother had begun a mighty undertaking.
She had drawn the lines,
My mother had done a wondrous thing,
My mother had begun the disruption.
My wretched mother had eight hundred pack-camels saddled, hey.
My mother had their sacks and bags prepared,
My mother hired ample transport,
My mother had the face of the earth searched.
My mother, beyond Andijan,
This side of Amangen,
Under Khan Kokand's shelter,
This side of Samarkand,
Had Kuleshen searched out.
Kuleshen's fireclay,
She had that fireclay brought,
And bore the expense.
My mother brought it by hired transport.
The earth of Kuleshen
She had mixed in great vats.
Chopping cattle and goat hair,
She had it sprinkled into those vats.
Aksakalbai's son,
The strong Sart Aralbai,
And sixty men with hoes,
She had them tread the mud.
Levying a tribute upon the Kyrgyz,
She gathered six thousand gelded goats,
Slaughtered all six thousand,
Firing bricks, she built it firmly.
Until six centuries had passed,
My khan-father's mausoleum
Was built not to crumble, hey.
Slaughtering seven thousand gelded goats, hey,
Making a model for the face of the earth,
She baked bricks and built it strong, hey.
Until seven centuries had passed,
She built it to stand unbroken, hey.
My valiant mother Kanykei
Set designs in every place.
My poor, luckless mother
Made wonders of every kind.
“When the orphan comes tomorrow,
Let him enter this mausoleum,” she thought.
“Of me, his unfortunate mother,
Let him know this devotion, hey,” she thought.
“His father's deeds,
The havoc he wrought in Beijing,
Let my poor son see them,” she thought.
When my bloodthirsty father died,
When the people buried my father,
Sparing none of her wealth,
My noble, luckless mother
To Egypt and Baghdad
To her khoja, my wretched mother,
Giving him six swift horses,
Giving him a palm-sized letter,
And summoned ninety mullahs.
Of the ninety, ten died on the road;
When eighty arrived safely,
To my khan-father's treasury,
When they came to the warriors,
She had memorial scenes made within.
My father's deeds,
Leaving not a hair's breadth out,
She had them all depicted.
At the foot of the threshold,
By the outer doorway,
Her mount was Arbuurul;
My mother's bloody face,
Her bloodied face torn,
Her black hair loose
Upon her drooping dark head—
Bereft of her bloodthirsty husband,
My mother at thirty-two,
